title: Designing Reliable AI Features for Real Products
excerpt: A sample look at the product habits that make AI features useful: narrow scope, observable output, and a clear human fallback.

sections.heading: Start with a small, testable job
paragraphs: This sample article demonstrates the portfolio blog layout. It is illustrative content, not a report of a specific production system.

A useful AI feature begins with a bounded task and a measurable result. Define what a good response looks like, which inputs are allowed, and when the system should hand the decision back to a person.

sections.heading: Make uncertainty visible
paragraphs: AI output should not look more certain than it is. Show source context where possible, make review easy, and record failures so the team can improve the workflow.
Treat evaluation as part of delivery: keep representative examples, check regressions, and measure quality against the task rather than relying on an impressive demo.

sections.heading: Design the fallback first
paragraphs: Users need a clear path when a model is unavailable or a response needs review. A predictable fallback turns an experimental capability into a dependable product feature.

title: How Clear API Contracts Help Full-Stack Teams Move Faster
excerpt: A practical sample guide to aligning frontend and backend work around stable request shapes, useful errors, and shared examples.

sections.heading: Agree on the shape before wiring screens
paragraphs: This sample post is placeholder copy intended to preview the blog experience; it does not claim a particular project outcome.
A compact request and response example gives frontend and backend contributors a shared target. Include required fields, optional values, and the cases that should return an error.

sections.heading: Make errors part of the contract
paragraphs: A consistent error shape lets interfaces explain what went wrong and lets tests check behavior without guessing. Include stable codes for expected failures and avoid leaking implementation details.

sections.heading: Keep examples close to the code
paragraphs: Document the contract where the team can validate it. Lightweight schema validation and a few integration tests help detect drift before it reaches users.

title: A Practical Figma-to-Code Review Loop
excerpt: A sample workflow for translating design tokens and component states into a focused visual review instead of a last-minute pixel hunt.

sections.heading: Extract the rules, not just the screenshot
paragraphs: This illustrative article previews a design and is sample content only. It is not a published case study.
Before implementing a screen, identify the reusable rules behind it: spacing, color roles, typography, breakpoints, and interaction states. Encoding those rules as tokens makes later updates cheaper.

sections.heading: Review component states
paragraphs: A page can match a static screenshot and still fail in use. Review hover, focus, loading, empty, and narrow-screen states alongside the default layout.

sections.heading: Use focused visual checks
paragraphs: Compare a few representative viewport sizes and prioritize differences by user impact. Fix shared components and token mismatches before polishing isolated details.
